final_proof:
Let h:(0,1)→L⊆X be a diffeomorphism onto L, after reparametrizing the given open interval by a diffeomorphism with (0,1). In particular, h is continuous and injective.

Define the two end-accumulation sets

A = ⋂_{0<c<1} closure(h((0,c)))  and  B = ⋂_{0<c<1} closure(h((c,1))),

where closures are taken in X. We first prove

closure(L) \ L ⊆ A ∪ B.  (1)

Suppose p∈closure(L)\L but p∉A∪B. Since p∉A, there is c₀∈(0,1) such that p∉closure(h((0,c₀))); this remains true if c₀ is decreased. Similarly, because p∉B, there is d₀∈(0,1) such that p∉closure(h((d₀,1))); this remains true if d₀ is increased. We may therefore choose 0<c<d<1 such that

p∉closure(h((0,c)))  and  p∉closure(h((d,1))).

The set h([c,d]) is compact. Since a manifold is Hausdorff, h([c,d]) is closed in X, and it does not contain p because it is contained in L. Hence

F = closure(h((0,c))) ∪ h([c,d]) ∪ closure(h((d,1)))

is a closed subset of X containing L but not p. This contradicts p∈closure(L), proving (1).

We next show that A contains at most one point. Suppose instead that distinct points p,q lie in A. By the Hausdorff and locally Euclidean properties of the one-manifold X, there is a coordinate interval V containing p such that q∉closure(V) and the frontier ∂V=closure(V)\V consists of at most two points. Indeed, choose disjoint neighborhoods of p and q, take a chart about p, and within it take the inverse image of a sufficiently small open interval whose closed interval remains inside the chart. That closed coordinate interval is compact and hence closed in X, and its frontier consists of its two endpoints (or at most two points if manifolds with boundary are allowed).

For every c∈(0,1), the connected set h((0,c)) meets V, because p∈closure(h((0,c))). It also meets X\closure(V), because this is an open neighborhood of q and q∈closure(h((0,c))). A connected set meeting both V and X\closure(V) must meet ∂V.

Apply this with c=1/n for every sufficiently large integer n. Since ∂V has at most two points, some r∈∂V belongs to h((0,1/n)) for infinitely many n. Every such occurrence puts r in L, and injectivity gives r a unique preimage t=h⁻¹(r)>0. But r∈h((0,1/n)) implies t<1/n. This cannot hold for infinitely many arbitrarily large n. Therefore |A|≤1.

The identical argument at the right-hand end, using the connected tails h((c,1)) as c tends to 1, proves |B|≤1. Combining this with (1),

|closure(L)\L| ≤ |A|+|B| ≤ 2.

Thus the closure of L contains at most two points not belonging to L.
